results.title: What is Linux distros (Linux distribution)? | Definition from TechTarget
results.content: # What is Linux distros (Linux distribution)? Linux distributions, which are based on the Linux kernel, are often easier for users to deploy than the open source version of Linux. Because Linux has open-source software at its core, every commercial company that has a paid distro must also have a free version, often called *community version*. ## Linux distro packages. A single Linux distribution could contain thousands of software packages. A Linux distribution also includes a package management system, or packet manager, which is used to install, uninstall and manage software packages. ## Linux distro families. Because most Linux distributions are released as open source, it is possible to take one distro as the core and release it as a new one with modifications. results.content: These may be patches or minor version updates of software you installed previously. For example, the distribution may suggest to upgrade firefox version 23 to firefox version 24 (bad example this is not a minor release but you get the idea). After a few months, though, the system asks you to do an upgrade : you're updating the system itself, not the software packages you have installed. Why can't the system itself be updated the same way as other software packages, via small, continuous updates ? What solution do rolling releases use to solve this problem ? * There was some good discussions on rolling releases in this U&L Q&A from a while back, titled: What is the prefered way of updating all software in a Fedora installation?. * *Why can't the system itself be updated the same way as other software packages, via small, continuous updates ?* It's a tradeoff: *bleeding edge* (rolling release) vs unchanging *known quantity* (stable distro version). ## 1 Answer 1. > Why can't the system itself be updated the same way as other software packages, via small, continuous updates ? The process of upgrading essentially is a set of updates; your distinction between "updating the system itself" and "not the software packages you have installed" is a little imprecise since the system *is* just software packages you have installed. I don't think there is any specific technical reason at all for using version upgrades, and I doubt it would require much for a traditional versioning distro to convert to rolling release. AFAIK, it is just software *distributions* which use a rolling release model. Well, they use versioning with the packages. With versioned distros, packages actually have two versions associated with them, the package version and the distro version. results.title: What Is an Immutable Linux Distro, and Should You Use One?
results.content: # What Is an Immutable Linux Distro, and Should You Use One? * Immutable Linux distributions are read-only operating systems that don't allow writing to the root file system. * These distros are more secure, reliable, and stable than ordinary Linux distros but also more complex to use. ## What Is an Immutable Linux Distribution? An immutable Linux distribution is an operating system (OS) that is read-only at its core. ## What Are the Advantages of Immutable Distros? Why should someone consider an immutable Linux distribution over regular ones? Immutable Linux distributions offer an additional layer of security by preventing unauthorized modifications to the system, making them more resistant to attacks. But in immutable distros, even the administrator can't modify the system files. ## How Does Software Installation and Updates Work on Immutable Distros? If immutable distros are read-only, how do you install applications or update them? Most, if not all, immutable distros use Flatpak, AppImages, or Snaps for managing software, which are self-contained package systems. Some immutable distributions use a technique known as "layering" to install packages. ## Best Use Cases for Immutable Distros. In fact, Steam Deck uses an immutable Arch Linux-based distribution called SteamOS. Likewise, a lot of handheld devices make use of immutable distros due to atomic updates. Immutable Linux distros are often used for containerized environments (like Docker and Kubernetes) to make sure you can maintain and scale applications in a predictable and consistent container runtime environment. ## Drawbacks of Immutable Linux Distros. Even if you're already experienced with Linux systems, you still need to learn about things that immutable distros do differently. If you want to install apps not available as Flatpaks or other universal formats, you need to install a whole new distro in a container just to use a single app. ## 4 Immutable Linux Distributions to Get You Started. NixOS is a completely reproducible immutable Linux distro. ## Is an Immutable Distro Right for You? So should you use an immutable distro? But for regular desktop use, immutable distros may not be a good choice. Some of the advantages that immutable distros come with are also available in regular Linux distros.

results.title: What is the proper way to use `pkg-config` from `cmake`? - Stack Overflow
results.content: # What is the proper way to use `pkg-config` from `cmake`? include(FindPkgConfig) pkg_search_module(SDL2 REQUIRED sdl2) target_include_directories(app SYSTEM PUBLIC ${SDL2_INCLUDE_DIRS}) target_link_libraries(app ${SDL2_LIBRARIES}). However, that seems to be the wrong way about doing it, as it only uses the include directories and libraries, but ignores defines, library paths and other flags that might be returned by `pkg-config`. target_link_libraries(testapp ${SDL2_LIBRARIES}) target_include_directories(testapp PUBLIC ${SDL2_INCLUDE_DIRS}) target_compile_options(testapp PUBLIC ${SDL2_CFLAGS_OTHER}). While I would really recommend to use the IMPORTED\_TARGET approach used in stackoverflow.com/a/57224542/211520, if you really need to `target_link_libraries()` then please use `_LINK_LIBRARIES` instead of just `_LIBRARIES`: The former has the full, absolute paths and thus works for non-standard directories too; for example when cross-compiling. If you're using cmake and pkg-config in a pretty normal way, this solution works. Another issue could be that the pkg-config files are not installed in the normal place, and the pkg-config paths for the project need to be added using the `PKG_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable while cmake is running (see other Stack Overflow questions regarding this). This solution also works well when you use the correct pkg-config path. cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.14) project(ya-project C) # the `pkg_check_modules` function is created with this call find_package(PkgConfig REQUIRED) # these calls create special `PkgConfig::` variables pkg_check_modules(MY_PKG REQUIRED IMPORTED_TARGET GLOBAL any-package) pkg_check_modules(YOUR_PKG REQUIRED IMPORTED_TARGET GLOBAL ya-package) add_executable(program-name file.c ya.c) target_link_libraries(program-name PUBLIC PkgConfig::MY_PKG PkgConfig::YOUR_PKG). Most of the available answers fail to configure the headers for the `pkg-config` library. include(FindPkgConfig) if(NOT PKG_CONFIG_FOUND) message(FATAL_ERROR "pkg-config not found!" ) endif() pkg_check_modules( REQUIRED IMPORTED_TARGET ) target_link_libraries( PkgConfig::). # sdl2 linking variables find_package(PkgConfig REQUIRED) pkg_check_modules(SDL2 REQUIRED sdl2 SDL2_ttf SDL2_mixer SDL2_image) # your app file(GLOB SRC "my_app/*.c") add_executable(my_app ${SRC}) target_link_libraries(my_app ${SDL2_LIBRARIES}) target_include_directories(my_app PUBLIC ${SDL2_INCLUDE_DIRS}) target_compile_options(my_app PUBLIC ${SDL2_CFLAGS_OTHER}). For me, `target_link_libraries(my_app ${SDL2_LINK_LIBRARIES})` worked better. pkg_check_modules(GTKGL REQUIRED gtkglext-1.0) include_directories(${GTKGL_INCLUDE_DIRS}) link_directories(${GTKGL_LIBRARY_DIRS}) add_definitions(${GTKGL_CFLAGS_OTHER}) set(LIBS ${LIBS} ${GTKGL_LIBRARIES}) target_link_libraries([insert name of program] ${LIBS}). 1") Linking libraries using Cmake - not used directly. 0") Avoid bad include paths in CMake's pkg-config fallback. results.content: What Linux distro am I running? If you mean to say what is the best Linux Distro which can be tuned to give better performance then there are many. What Linux distro has the best software manager? Do different Linux Distros have different performance? Linux is not an operating system like Windows, where you have to use what you get and live with it. Therefore it’s a Linux distro, right? So, if one Linux distribution performs way better than the other, because it’s way leaner than the other and comes with a severe lack of features and not even a GUI, would you now use this distro instead and daily? What is the best Linux distro in 2020? It’s literally about DISTRIBUTING a certain set of features and settings, based on the Linux operating system kernel, to other people. It’s a Linux-based modular software system, that comes with a certain set of features and settings, for a particular purpose and taste and is being distributed in this particular configuration to like-minded people. Linux distributions can come with different (graphical or text-based) user interfaces, different hardware drivers, different applications out of the box, different additional software in the default software repositories, different package management system for installing, removing and managing software, they can use different models for upgrades… Meaning, the different distributions can look different, feel different, handle different, perform different. Linux, the kernel itself would probably be something like a foundation you build everything on, the software packages would be the bricks and components and the Linux distributions are the houses and airplanes and space vehicles and cars and… ;) Depending on the parts you choose and what you make of it, the systems cater to different purpose, taste and working style.
